frameworks.name: Three Ways to 10x Income
frameworks.definition: A three-part framework for income multiplication: (1) arbitrage — exploit price differentials between markets; (2) giveaways — give away outsized value to generate demand then monetize a back-end product; (3) price anchoring — raise perceived value of existing offers by placing a premium anchor tier above them.

frameworks.name: Lead Magnet Types
frameworks.definition: Three structural forms for free-value giveaways: (a) reveal a problem — surface a gap the prospect didn't know they had; (b) free trial — let them sample the core product; (c) one-step solution to a multi-step problem — solve step one for free so the prospect naturally needs the remaining steps.

frameworks.name: Give Free, Monetize Differently
frameworks.definition: Hormozi's preferred business model: identify what competitors sell, make a better version free, then monetize via a separate back-end product that the free offer naturally leads to — reversing the conventional paid-then-deliver sequence.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that wealth is a ratio (income relative to spend), not an absolute number: a person earning $5,000/month who spends $500 feels richer than one earning $50,000/month who spends more than they earn. Geographic arbitrage is one mechanism — living in a low-cost country (e.g., Thailand median income ~$2,700/year) while selling services at US/European rates (~$50,000-$60,000/year) produces a 10x+ wealth ratio without increasing absolute income.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to employees and solopreneurs selling services globally
Requires English proficiency or a remotely sellable skill
Assumes low-cost country of residence and high-cost country of sale
claims.mechanism: The spread between cost-of-living and income-earned is the functional definition of wealth accumulation; reducing spend in a low-cost geography is economically equivalent to raising income.

numbers.axis: Annual income relative to cost of living by geography

bounded_by: Does not apply to capital-intensive businesses requiring physical presence
Network arbitrage (paying premium to live near wealthy people) is higher risk and not recommended by Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that geographic arbitrage (buying cheaply in one market, selling at premium in another) is the foundational economic mechanism underlying all profit: any business that earns more for a service than it costs to deliver is practicing arbitrage, whether or not the owner recognizes it as such.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Profit is defined as the spread between what a service costs to produce and what a buyer pays for it; framing this as arbitrage makes the lever visible and actionable at every income level.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the two most powerful words in marketing are 'free' and 'new,' and that giveaways are so effective they are government-regulated — citing regulation as evidence of the tactic's power.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a giveaway only generates durable demand if the free item has a real, hard cost that prospects can perceive — otherwise recipients do not feel genuine reciprocity and do not convert to buyers. A giveaway of something perceived as trivially cheap produces no reciprocity obligation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to lead magnets and free-value offers of all types
Especially relevant for info-product and service businesses
claims.mechanism: Perceived value of the free item triggers reciprocity; the recipient feels psychologically obligated to return value in the form of money. If the hard cost is invisible or the item seems cheap, no reciprocity impulse is created.
bounded_by: Does not apply to luxury goods where scarcity rather than reciprocity drives conversion

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a giveaway strategy will always remain available as a competitive advantage because fewer than 5% of businesses have the patience and discipline to execute it properly — the difficulty is behavioral (willingness to wait for monetization), not informational.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Assumes business has a monetizable back-end product or service
claims.mechanism: The strategy requires delayed monetization; most operators are unwilling to incur real upfront costs and wait for downstream returns, keeping effective competitors few.

numbers.axis: Share of businesses willing to execute the giveaway strategy

anchors.region: businesses who hear about it and do not act

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the three levers for 10x-ing a business are: getting 10x more customers, making each customer worth 10x more, and giving away outsized value to generate the demand needed for the first two. These three levers are independent and can each individually produce order-of-magnitude improvement.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to any business regardless of stage or size

numbers.axis: Magnitude of improvement required for 10x business growth

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that pricing is the single most powerful lever on profit: raising prices increases profit without increasing cost or volume, and it can be applied at any business stage from solopreneur to large business.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that employees can increase their income most significantly by switching to performance-based compensation (percentage or full commission tied to a metric they control), because tying compensation to revenue creation makes the employee's value directly visible and negotiable — and outperforms simply asking for a raise or switching companies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to employees in roles where output can be tied to revenue or profit
Easiest to implement in sales roles; requires creativity in non-sales roles
claims.mechanism: Employers pay for risk-taking; shifting compensation to performance-based transfers downside risk to the employee in exchange for uncapped upside. The closer an employee's output is tied to revenue, the more leverage they have in compensation negotiation.
bounded_by: Does not apply to roles where individual output cannot be plausibly connected to company revenue
Role-switching within the same company can match or exceed performance-comp gains in certain structures

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a price anchor — a premium-tier offer priced well above the core offer — causes buyers to perceive all lower tiers as more affordable by comparison, increasing conversion and average order value on the core tier even when very few buyers choose the anchor.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when the premium tier is presented before or alongside the base offer
Works in B2C and B2B contexts wherever pricing menus exist
claims.mechanism: Humans frame all numbers relative to the first number they hear; a high anchor makes the base price feel smaller by comparison, reducing purchase resistance on the main offer without changing its price.
bounded_by: Does not apply to commodity markets where price transparency removes anchoring effects

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that including large numbers early in any sales presentation — even numbers unrelated to price — increases buyers' willingness to accept higher prices later, because numbers heard first mentally frame the scale of all subsequent figures.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to any sales context with a structured pitch or presentation
claims.mechanism: Cognitive anchoring operates on the first number encountered; large early numbers set a high reference frame that makes subsequent prices seem proportionally smaller.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi distinguishes luxury products from premium products: luxury items derive value from the fact that their high price is publicly known (the price itself confers status), whereas premium products derive value from delivering meaningfully superior results or experiences. These are distinct pricing and positioning strategies.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: For luxury, conspicuous price is the product — higher price increases desirability because other people must know you paid it. For premium, the value proposition is the outcome delivered, not the price paid.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the product a business sells in the highest volume is often not the product it makes the most profit on; the profit-maximizing product is typically a higher-margin add-on or premium tier sold to the same customer. He cites McDonald's as the canonical example: burgers drive traffic but Coke and fries generate disproportionate margin.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies to businesses with multi-product portfolios or tiered offers
claims.mechanism: High-volume core products have lower margins due to production complexity; high-margin add-ons (beverages, fries, premium tiers) ride on the acquisition cost already paid by the core product, making their incremental profit disproportionate.
bounded_by: Does not apply to single-product businesses with no upsell path

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that adding a premium 10x-priced tier to an existing offer (e.g., $5,000/month alongside a $500/month core) produces two simultaneous effects: (a) some buyers purchase the premium tier directly, generating unexpected high-margin revenue; (b) the previously most expensive package becomes perceived as the affordable middle option, increasing its conversion rate.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when a 10x premium tier is genuinely deliverable, even if infrequently
More effective in B2C and high-touch service contexts
claims.mechanism: Three-tier presentation creates a reference point effect: the premium anchor elevates perceived value of the middle tier and suppresses perceived cost by making it appear to be the moderate, reasonable option.

numbers.axis: Price ratio of anchor tier to base tier

bounded_by: Premium tier must be genuinely deliverable; fake anchors erode trust

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that leveraging an existing customer or contact list is the highest-ROI growth lever because customer acquisition cost has already been incurred — any revenue generated from an existing list is essentially zero-marginal-cost revenue.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Requires an existing customer email list, phone contacts, or social following
Applies after new giveaway and premium anchor tier are in place
claims.mechanism: CAC is already spent on existing contacts; additional revenue from those contacts costs only the marginal cost of communication and fulfillment, making the incremental margin structure extremely favorable.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi contends that a three-email campaign to an existing large list — driving recipients to a webinar where a compelling offer is presented — can produce millions in revenue at near-zero incremental cost. He cites a portfolio company that generated $2.3 million from such a campaign.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Requires a large email list (the cited example had millions of subscribers)
Requires a proven compelling offer to present at the webinar
Incremental cost is minimal only when list is already built and offer already exists

numbers.axis: Revenue generated per email campaign to existing list, scaled by list size

bounded_by: Assumes the list was legitimately built with engaged subscribers
Results not reproducible from cold or low-engagement lists

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that the free giveaway must naturally lead to a problem that the paid back-end product solves; without this logical connection, the giveaway generates goodwill but not revenue. Each of his giveaway examples revealed a gap that his paid product directly filled.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Applies when designing a giveaway or lead magnet
Required for giveaway economics to close: giveaway costs must be offset by back-end conversion
claims.mechanism: The giveaway solves step one of a multi-step problem; the prospect, now more aware of remaining steps, is primed to pay for the solution to steps two through N. Without this sequential structure, the giveaway is charitable but not commercially productive.
bounded_by: Does not apply if the giveaway is a standalone product with no natural extension

examples.text: A founder Hormozi met in his building's elevator pitched him on a software business and showed a prototype on his phone during the elevator ride. Hormozi went to dinner with him and ultimately invested. When asked how the founder could afford to live in the high-rise, he said: 'I can't afford not to live here because I get to meet people like you.' The founder was using network arbitrage — intentionally overpaying for proximity to wealthy individuals — to fund the company's growth entirely through relationships made in the building. The company became successful. Hormozi notes this strategy worked but is unusually risky and not his recommended approach.

When Hormozi started his first gym, he lived on the floor and then in a shared spare bedroom for $400/month, had $50,000 saved, and was making $4,000/month from online training. He shopped exclusively at Costco to minimize food costs. This personal expense arbitrage freed capital for aggressive business reinvestment even before the gym opened.

Hormozi's six-week challenge at his gym gave away six full weeks of service — accountability, workouts, and nutrition planning — when competitors offered only 14- to 21-day trials with partial services. Participants paid upfront but received the money back if they completed the program, which encouraged sign-ups. This took the gym to a completely different growth trajectory compared to traditional marketing approaches.

Hormozi wrote Gym Launch Secrets — a 400-page book covering everything needed to run a gym, including trainer ads, sales scripts, lobby setup, upsell processes, pricing packages, and semi-private training. He was afraid to publish it because it contained all his operational knowledge, but Layla Hormozi encouraged him by saying 'if you're afraid it's too good, it's probably the right thing to give away.' After publication, his sales team reported that prospects who had read the book required almost no selling — they arrived already bought into the Gym Launch method and just wanted help implementing it.

When launching Allen, his software company, Hormozi gave away unlimited coaching, training, and a full agency-growth course to anyone who used the software. Competitors were charging significant fees for similar information. This resulted in Allen growing from zero to $1.7 million per month in revenue within six months, driven entirely by inbound demand from the free giveaway.

For Prestige Labs, his supplement company, Hormozi created S3 (Supplement Selling Secrets) — a selling system he had used profitably for years — and gave it away free to anyone who sold his supplements. He priced Prestige products so that gym owners who went through the free training had better economics using Prestige than competitor supplements. While some recipients used the selling system with other brands, the training was specifically designed to lead naturally to Prestige's product features, so most converted.

At Nuseret (Salt Bae's steakhouse chain), regular steaks are priced around $90-$100 — already expensive by steakhouse standards. The gold menu wraps steaks in gold foil and charges $2,000-$3,000. The gold items sell not because they taste better but because the buyer wants others to know they spent that amount — the high price is the product. This illustrates the luxury distinction: the price itself confers the value via public status signaling, unlike premium products where value comes from superior outcomes.

A friend of Hormozi's who ran a B2C online business at $500/month created a new premium 1-on-1 version priced at $5,000/month — 10x the core offer — with no expectation that many would buy it. The result: some buyers did choose the $5,000 tier, generating unexpected high-margin revenue. Additionally, conversion on the previously most expensive package increased because it now appeared as the affordable middle option in a three-tier menu rather than the most expensive choice.

Hormozi's largest portfolio company ran a three-email campaign to their multi-million subscriber list, directing recipients to a webinar presenting a compelling offer. The campaign generated $2.3 million in revenue. Hormozi notes the incremental cost was near zero because the list had already been built and the offer already existed.

McDonald's core product is burgers, but burgers generate thin margins due to meat, bun, lettuce, tomatoes, onions, and other fresh ingredients. Coke and fries carry significantly higher margins, making them the true profit maximizers. McDonald's corporate's primary business is actually real estate (from franchisees), but at the franchisee level, the Coke, ice cream, and fries category generates the disproportionate share of profit even though burgers drive traffic volume.

practices.text: Raise prices before trying any other growth lever. Pricing is the fastest path to increased profit because it requires no additional customers or cost.
Write a book before entering any new market. The writing process forces consolidation and synthesis of knowledge, producing both a learning artifact and a giveaway that pre-sells prospects.
Design every giveaway to reveal a problem that your paid product solves, so recipients naturally move toward purchasing without a hard sell.
When in a salaried employee role, switch to performance-based compensation tied to a metric you control before negotiating a raise or switching companies.
Include large numbers early in any sales presentation — before the price — to prime the buyer's reference frame for higher absolute figures.

Before seeking new customers, send an email campaign to your existing contact list (email contacts, phone contacts, social followers) offering a new high-value free item plus an upsell, since acquisition cost for that audience is already sunk.
